sentence: The mode, the most common value, can sit far from both mean and median in a skewed distribution. For household income the mode lies low, near where the bulk of households cluster, while the mean is dragged high by the tail. Three perfectly legitimate notions of center give three different numbers, and choosing among them is itself a substantive decision about what typical should mean.

Forecasting exploits autocorrelation: the more a series remembers its past, the further ahead a useful prediction can reach. A series that is essentially white noise offers nothing beyond its mean to forecast with. The strength and reach of the autocorrelation set a ceiling on how much skill any forecast, however sophisticated, can possibly extract.

An analyst with a dataset and no significant result tries another outcome variable, then drops a few inconvenient observations, then adds a covariate, then switches to a one-sided test. Somewhere in this sequence a p-value slips below the threshold. Each move was defensible alone, but the search across them, unrecorded, turned a null dataset into a publishable finding.

Aggregation can inflate correlations dramatically. Averaging within groups smooths away individual scatter, so a weak individual-level relationship can appear as a strong one between group means. A correlation of 0.3 among people can become 0.9 among regional averages, and reporting the regional figure as if it described people overstates the link severalfold.

Saying the result was significant, so we accept the alternative hypothesis, mishandles the logic of the test. The procedure rejects the null or fails to reject it; it never affirms a specific alternative. The data are equally compatible with many alternatives near the estimate, and the test alone provides no warrant for singling out the one the analyst happened to favor before collecting data.

Seasonality masquerades as trend if not removed. Retail sales always climb toward December, so a rise from October to December signals the calendar, not growth. Comparing each month against the same month a year earlier, or applying a seasonal adjustment, separates the recurring pattern from a genuine underlying movement.

The law tells us the sample mean converges but says nothing about how fast. Convergence can be slow, especially for heavy-tailed distributions where rare enormous values keep nudging the running average. Knowing that the mean will eventually settle is cold comfort if eventually means a sample size far beyond what any experiment can collect.

The fallacy thrives because a tiny probability sounds conclusive. But a small chance of the evidence given innocence is only half the comparison. If the evidence is also somewhat unlikely under guilt, or if guilt was extremely improbable to begin with, the posterior probability of guilt can remain far from certainty despite the headline-grabbing rarity.

The bias-variance tradeoff lies behind overfitting. A model too simple is biased, missing the real pattern. A model too complex has high variance, swinging wildly with each new sample. The sweet spot minimizes the sum, and cross-validation is the practical instrument for locating it without peeking at the data reserved for the final verdict.

When a rare event has not been observed at all, the data give a count of zero, and the naive estimate of its probability is zero. That cannot be right for an event known to be possible. A rule of thumb places an upper bound near three divided by the number of trials, so a hundred clean trials still leave room for a true rate as high as three percent.

Two factories ship parts with the same mean diameter, yet one is far more reliable. The difference lives entirely in the variance. A small spread means most parts hug the target; a large spread means many stray, and the customer rejecting out-of-tolerance parts feels the variance, not the mean. A summary that reports only the average misses what matters most here.

subtopic: Type I and Type II errors
sentence: Four factors determine the two error rates jointly: the significance threshold, the sample size, the true effect size, and the variability of the data. Fix three and the fourth follows. Power analysis exploits this arithmetic, solving for the sample size that holds the Type II error at an acceptable level given a worst-case effect worth detecting.

subtopic: Type I and Type II errors
sentence: The cost asymmetry should drive the design. Screening for a treatable but deadly disease makes a missed case far worse than a false alarm, so the test is tuned for high sensitivity even at the price of many Type I errors. Where the follow-up is itself dangerous, the balance tips the other way. The error rates are levers, and which to favor is an ethical and economic decision, not a statistical one.

A game show host hides a prize behind one of three doors. After the contestant picks, the host opens a different door revealing no prize and offers a switch. The intuitive answer that it now makes no difference is wrong. The contestant's first pick wins one time in three; switching wins the other two, because the host's informed action redistributes the conditional probability.

Bayesian methods can be especially valuable with small samples, because a sensibly chosen prior supplies information that the scant data cannot. Where a frequentist interval would sprawl uselessly wide, a prior built from related studies or domain knowledge anchors the estimate, provided the analyst is candid that the conclusion now leans partly on that prior.

Ecological data are not worthless; they are simply answering an ecological question. The mistake is only in the transfer of the conclusion to individuals. A study of regional pollution and regional disease rates legitimately informs policy at the regional scale, and reported as such it is sound. It becomes a fallacy the moment it is read as a claim about exposed persons.

The normal distribution is fixed entirely by two numbers, its mean and its standard deviation. Every normal curve is a shifted, stretched copy of the standard one. This two-parameter simplicity is why so much classical statistics assumes normality: once those two numbers are estimated, the whole distribution, and every probability it implies, is determined.

Comparing spreads across different scales calls for the coefficient of variation, the standard deviation divided by the mean. A spread of ten dollars is large for coffee prices and trivial for car prices. Expressing variability relative to the mean makes a meaningful comparison possible between quantities measured in incomparable magnitudes.

Recall bias distorts questions about the past. People asked to remember how often they did something months ago misremember, and the misremembering is often systematic, with memorable events overcounted and routine ones forgotten. When the recall error differs between groups being compared, it can manufacture a difference that the underlying behavior does not have.

A spam filter is a running Bayesian update. Each word in an incoming message carries a likelihood ratio learned from past mail, and the filter multiplies these together against a prior odds of spam. The final posterior odds decide the verdict, and every message the user labels feeds back to refine the word-level likelihoods for next time.

Survival methods reach far beyond medicine. The time until a machine fails, until a customer cancels a subscription, until a released prisoner reoffends, all are time-to-event data with censoring, because some machines still run and some customers have not yet left. The same Kaplan-Meier curves and hazard models apply wherever the question is how long until something happens.

Controlling the family-wise error rate and controlling the false discovery rate answer different questions. The first guards against even a single false positive and suits confirmatory work where one mistake is costly. The second tolerates a controlled proportion of false positives among discoveries and suits exploratory screens where missing real signals is the greater danger. The choice depends on what comes after the test.

Censoring must be unrelated to the prognosis for the analysis to stay honest. If sicker patients drop out and are censored precisely because they are about to have the event, the remaining subjects look healthier than the true population, and the survival curve is biased upward. This informative censoring breaks the assumption every standard method relies on.

Color carries meaning, and choosing it carelessly misleads. A rainbow palette implies an ordering its hues do not naturally possess, and a red-green scheme excludes the colorblind. A sequential palette should run light to dark for ordered data; a diverging one should center on a meaningful midpoint. The color scale is a quiet but consequential analytic choice.

Online reviews of a service are written by people who chose to use it and chose to write, two selection filters stacked. The visible ratings describe a population shaped by both choices, not the general public. A service could be loved by its self-selected users and ill-suited to everyone else, and the review average would never reveal it.

Sometimes the pattern of missingness is itself informative. An unanswered question about drug use, or a blank where income should be, may carry signal about the respondent. Treating the missingness indicator as a variable in its own right can recover that signal, turning the gap from a pure nuisance into a piece of data.

A subtle error voids cross-validation: performing feature selection on the full dataset before splitting. The selection has already seen the held-out points, so the validation no longer measures performance on truly unseen data. Every step that learns from the data, including selection and tuning, must sit inside the cross-validation loop.

Degrees of freedom shrink fast in small samples, and with them the reliability of variance-based inference. A t-test on five observations has four degrees of freedom, and the critical value sits far out in the tail, demanding a large effect before significance is reached. The arithmetic itself enforces caution when data are scarce.

Dropping every record with any missing field, the default in many analyses, quietly shrinks the sample and can bias it. If older patients are likelier to skip a question, the complete cases skew young. The convenience of complete-case analysis hides a selection step, and that step is harmless only under the strongest of the missingness mechanisms.

There exist pathological cases where a valid confidence interval can be empty or can contain every possible value, yet still satisfy its long-run coverage guarantee. Such intervals are technically correct and practically absurd. They dramatize that coverage is a property of the procedure, divorced from whether any single interval is informative about the parameter.

Whether to trust the aggregated trend or the within-group trends is not a statistical question but a causal one. If the grouping variable is a cause of both the exposure and the outcome, conditioning on it removes confounding and the within-group figures are right. If instead the grouping variable lies on the causal pathway, conditioning on it blocks part of the effect and the aggregate is the honest summary.

subtopic: publication bias and the file drawer
sentence: A meta-analysis is only as honest as the literature it pools. If unflattering studies are systematically missing, the meta-analysis inherits the bias and may even amplify it by lending the inflated estimate the authority of synthesis. Detecting and correcting for the missing studies is not optional polish; it is central to whether the pooled number means anything.

A famous early study correlated state-level suicide rates with the proportion of Protestants and concluded that Protestants were more prone to suicide. The grouped data could not establish which individuals took their lives. The conclusion may hold, but it does not follow from the aggregate correlation, and that gap is the ecological fallacy in its original form.

A double-barreled question asks two things at once and forces a single answer. Asking whether the staff were friendly and efficient leaves no clean reply for a respondent who found them friendly but slow. The answer that results is uninterpretable, and the only fix is to split the question into its separate parts.

The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with a constant success probability. The moment the trials become dependent, or the probability drifts between them, the binomial no longer applies, and treating overdispersed proportion data as binomial produces standard errors that are too small and confidence that is unearned.

Permutation tests offer a clean route for small samples, because with few observations the full set of label rearrangements can be enumerated exactly. The resulting p-value makes no distributional assumption and carries no approximation error, which is precisely the reassurance a scarce, hard-won handful of data points most needs.

The Cox proportional hazards model relates covariates to the hazard without committing to a shape for the baseline hazard itself. Its key assumption is that a covariate multiplies the hazard by a constant factor at all times. If a treatment helps early and harms late, that proportionality is violated, and the single hazard ratio the model reports becomes misleading.

Length-biased sampling distorts estimates of duration. If you arrive at a bus stop at a random moment and measure the gap between buses you happen to land in, you are more likely to fall inside a long gap than a short one, simply because long gaps occupy more of the timeline. The average gap you sample exceeds the average gap the schedule actually contains.

Cross-validation tunes a model, but tuning extensively against the cross-validation score can itself overfit to that score. The remedy is a final, untouched test set, locked away until the model is fully chosen. The test set is spent once, and the number it returns is the only estimate not contaminated by the search that produced the model.

When prosecutors cite a one-in-a-million chance of a random DNA match, jurors may treat that as the probability of innocence. It is not. In a database of millions, several innocent people could match by coincidence. The match probability per person must be combined with the size of the searched pool, and neglecting that base rate inflates the apparent strength of the evidence.

Expectation is linear, which makes it powerful. The expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values, whether or not the parts are independent. To find the expected number of people who get their own hat back from a shuffled pile, sum the tiny chance for each person, and the answer falls out as exactly one, with no need to untangle the dependence.

An investor who picks the funds with the best five-year returns is selecting partly on skill and partly on luck. Because luck does not persist, the chosen funds tend to underperform their past selves afterward. The expected future return regresses toward the average of the comparable pool, and the gap between the dazzling track record and the modest sequel is the predictable cost of having selected on an extreme.

A common pitfall is to set the target effect size to whatever the researcher hopes is true rather than to the smallest effect that would matter. Powering a study for an optimistic effect produces a sample too small to detect the modest but still important effect that nature actually provides, and the study then fails to inform the decision it was meant to support.

Reliability sets a ceiling on validity. An instrument cannot correlate with anything more strongly than it correlates with itself. If a depression scale has a reliability of 0.6, its correlation with any outcome is capped well below one, and a researcher chasing a stronger association is chasing a number the noisy measure can never reach.

Differential measurement error is more dangerous than random error. If cases recall their past exposures more diligently than controls, the error is not symmetric noise but a systematic distortion tied to the outcome. Such recall bias can create an association out of nothing or hide a real one, and unlike random error it does not merely attenuate, it deceives.

Inter-rater reliability matters whenever humans score the data. If two judges rating the same essays disagree often, the score reflects which judge happened to grade it as much as the essay's quality. Statistics like Cohen's kappa quantify agreement beyond chance, and a low value means the measurement is contaminated by the rater rather than determined by the thing rated.

Engineers studying returning warplanes mapped the bullet holes and proposed armoring the most-hit areas. The holes, however, marked where a plane could be struck and still come home. The unarmored spots in the data were the spots that, when hit, brought planes down before they could be sampled. The reinforcement belonged precisely where the returning aircraft showed no damage at all.

A famous 1936 prediction of a landslide for the losing candidate came from a survey of millions, drawn from telephone directories and car registrations. In the depths of the Depression, owning a phone and a car marked an unrepresentative, wealthier slice of voters. The enormous sample size could not rescue an estimate built on a frame that systematically excluded the poor.

Pretesting a questionnaire on a small group exposes the questions that confuse, offend, or mislead before the full survey is fielded. Cognitive interviews, in which respondents think aloud while answering, reveal whether they interpret each item as the designer intended. A survey launched without pretesting may collect thousands of answers to questions that were never understood.

A correlation can also arise from selection into the sample. Among hospitalized patients, two unrelated diseases may appear negatively correlated, because having either one raises the chance of admission and conditioning on admission induces a spurious association. The link is an artifact of who got into the dataset, not a feature of the diseases themselves.

Framing the same statistic as a gain or a loss changes how it is received. Saying a surgery has a ninety percent survival rate reassures, while saying it has a ten percent mortality rate alarms, though the numbers are identical. An honest presentation gives both framings, since the choice of frame is itself a form of persuasion.

The p-value measures compatibility between data and a specific null model, including every auxiliary assumption baked into that model. A small value can flag a genuine effect, but it can equally flag a violated independence assumption, a mis-specified error distribution, or selective reporting. Pinning the surprise entirely on the parameter of interest, while ignoring the assumptions traveling alongside it, is one of the most common errors in applied work.

Analyzing a cluster sample as if it were a simple random sample is a common and costly mistake. The standard errors come out too small, the confidence intervals too narrow, and findings look more certain than the data warrant. Software that accounts for the survey design exists precisely so the inference respects how the sample was actually drawn.

Centering continuous predictors before forming an interaction term improves interpretability. With raw variables, the main-effect coefficients describe the effect at the arbitrary point zero, which may lie outside the data. Centered at the mean, those coefficients describe the effect for an average individual, a far more meaningful reference point.

Response options anchor the answer. When asked how many hours of television they watch, respondents given a scale topping out at more than four hours report higher viewing than those given a scale topping out at more than two and a half, because the scale itself signals what is normal. The options offered shape the answer collected.

Expected value guides repeated decisions far better than one-off ones. A casino playing millions of hands relies on its small per-hand edge converging to a near-certain profit. A gambler playing a handful of hands faces a distribution wide enough that the expectation tells him little about his actual night, and a single session can stray far from the mean.

The range, the gap between the largest and smallest values, is the crudest measure of spread and the most fragile. It depends on exactly two observations and grows mechanically as the sample size increases, since a bigger sample has more chances to catch an extreme. It conveys something at a glance but should never be the only spread reported.

Difference-in-differences exploits a comparison group to cancel confounders that are stable over time. If both a treated region and an untreated region would have followed parallel trends, then the change in the treated region beyond the change in the control isolates the treatment effect. The method's credibility hinges entirely on that parallel-trends assumption holding.

The crucial assumption that missingness depends only on observed data cannot be checked from the data themselves, because doing so would require the very values that are absent. The analyst must argue for it from knowledge of how the data were collected. Missing-data analysis therefore rests on a premise that is reasoned toward, never verified.

One mistyped data point, a salary entered as nine million instead of ninety thousand, can drag the mean of a small payroll far above every actual wage. The median ignores the error entirely, because it depends only on the rank of the middle value. When a single extreme observation can hijack a summary, the resistant statistic is the safer report.

subtopic: publication bias and the file drawer
sentence: The fail-safe number asks how many unpublished null studies would have to exist to overturn a meta-analytic finding. If a handful of buried nulls could erase the effect, the conclusion is fragile. If thousands would be needed, the file drawer would have to be implausibly stuffed, and the result stands more securely against the unseen literature.

Whether a point counts as an outlier depends on the assumed distribution. A value four standard deviations from the mean is shocking under a normal model and unremarkable under a heavy-tailed one. Before flagging extremes, the analyst must ask whether the model expects rare large values, because outlier is a verdict relative to a distribution, not an absolute property.

Natural frequencies make risk comprehensible where probabilities confuse. Telling someone that, of a hundred patients like them, four will develop the condition and ninety-six will not, communicates more clearly than a four percent probability. The shift from abstract proportions to counted people aligns the statistic with how the mind reasons about chance.

A confidence interval that includes zero is routinely described as showing no effect, but it equally includes a range of non-zero effects that may matter. The interval running from minus one to eight units does not say the effect is absent; it says the data are consistent with anything from a small harm to a substantial benefit. The honest reading is uncertainty, not nullity.

Engineers propagate uncertainty through a complex formula by Monte Carlo. Each uncertain input is given a distribution, thousands of input sets are drawn, the formula is evaluated on each, and the spread of outputs reveals how input uncertainty flows into output uncertainty. Where an analytic error propagation would be hopeless, the simulation simply does the experiment in software.

Random measurement error in a predictor biases a regression slope toward zero, an effect called attenuation. The noise spreads the predictor out without spreading the outcome correspondingly, flattening the apparent relationship. A real effect can look weak not because it is weak but because the instrument that measured the cause was imprecise.

A boxplot draws its whiskers at a conventional distance from the quartiles and marks anything beyond as a candidate outlier. The rule is a useful screen, not a law. In a large sample some points will fall outside the whiskers by pure chance even when nothing is wrong, so the marks invite inspection rather than automatic deletion.

A study reports that coffee drinkers have higher rates of lung disease. Before blaming coffee, note that heavy coffee drinkers in that era were also heavy smokers. Smoking is a common cause of both the exposure and the outcome, and an analysis that does not adjust for it hands coffee the blame that belongs to tobacco.

Pre-registration blunts the multiple comparisons problem by fixing the analysis before the data arrive. Once the primary outcome, the subgroups, and the model are committed in advance, the analyst can no longer wander the space of options choosing whatever crosses the line. The p-value then means what it claims, because the number of tests is pinned down rather than expanding silently during analysis.

A celebrated wrongful conviction turned on the claim that the chance of two infant deaths in one family by natural causes was one in seventy-three million. The figure assumed the two deaths were independent and ignored the prior rarity of the alternative, deliberate harm. Comparing the likelihood of the evidence under each hypothesis, not quoting one figure alone, is the only sound way to weigh it.

The defense attorney's fallacy is the mirror image. Hearing that ten people in the city share the forensic profile, the defense argues the defendant has only a one-in-ten chance of guilt. But the other evidence in the case has already narrowed the field, and the profile match must be combined with that context, not used to dilute it down to a bare count.

An online experiment shows the new checkout flow converts worse overall, yet better on both desktop and mobile considered separately. The rollout coincided with a marketing push that drove a surge of low-intent mobile visitors. Device mix changed between the variants, so the pooled rate compares populations that differ in baseline conversion, not just in the feature being tested.

The right level of analysis is the level at which the question lives. If the question is whether an individual's diet affects their individual health, individual data are required. If the question is whether a city's food policy affects the city's outcomes, city-level data are appropriate. Mismatching the data's level to the question's level is the source of the error.

Recruiting study participants through a university bulletin board yields mostly young, educated, urban volunteers. Conclusions drawn from them are sound for that group but travel poorly to retirees or rural populations. The convenience of the sample is bought with a loss of generality, and any claim about people in general must be hedged by who actually walked through the door.

The expected value of a function of a random variable is generally not the function of the expected value. The expected square of a die roll is not the square of three and a half. This inequality, a form of Jensen's inequality, trips up analysts who substitute an average into a nonlinear formula and treat the output as an expectation.

Searching a dataset for any subgroup where the effect differs is the multiple comparisons problem wearing the costume of interaction analysis. Test enough interactions and one will reach significance by chance. An interaction discovered by such a search is a hypothesis for the next study, not a finding, unless it was specified in advance with a reason.

When the data have a time order, residuals plotted in sequence should not show runs or cycles. A residual that tends to be followed by a residual of the same sign betrays autocorrelation, meaning the observations are not independent. The model's standard errors then understate the uncertainty, and a time-aware error structure is needed.

Truncation discards observations entirely when a variable falls outside a range; censoring keeps them but with incomplete information. A study of incomes above a threshold is truncated, and its sample mean overstates the population mean. Recognizing whether data are truncated or censored decides which correction the analysis must apply.

The ecological fallacy is the error of inferring individual relationships from group averages. A correlation between a country's average income and its average happiness says something about countries. Whether richer individuals are happier is a separate question, answerable only with individual-level data, and the group correlation cannot settle it.

Risk is rarely a single number for everyone. A population-average risk of five percent may hide a high-risk tenth carrying most of the danger and a low-risk majority facing almost none. Quoting the average to an individual can badly misinform, because the individual sits somewhere on a distribution that the headline figure has flattened.

An intervention that significantly raises test scores by two points on a hundred-point scale has cleared a statistical bar but may not have cleared an educational one. Whether two points justifies the program's cost is a question of values and resources, not of p-values. Statistical significance is a screening filter; practical significance is the decision that follows.

Heteroscedasticity, residual spread that changes across the range of predictions, does not bias the fitted coefficients but corrupts their standard errors. A model that predicts small values precisely and large values loosely will report uncertainty that is wrong in both regions. Robust standard errors or a variance-stabilizing transformation are the usual repairs.

Matching pairs each treated subject with an untreated one alike on the measured confounders, so the comparison holds those variables fixed. It is intuitive and transparent, but it controls only what was matched on, and subjects who find no suitable match are dropped, narrowing the population to which the conclusion applies.

Simulating rare events efficiently requires more than waiting for them to happen. Importance sampling deliberately tilts the simulation toward the rare region, then reweights the results to undo the tilt. A naive simulation might run for years before a one-in-a-billion event appears even once; the reweighted scheme estimates its probability in a fraction of the runs.

To check whether a statistical test behaves as advertised, simulate. Generate thousands of datasets under the null hypothesis, run the test on each, and tally how often it falsely rejects. If the rejection rate matches the nominal level, the test is calibrated; if it strays, the test's assumptions are violated in the simulated regime, and a warning has been earned cheaply.

Subgroup analysis is a multiple comparisons problem in disguise. A trial that finds no overall effect but a significant benefit in left-handed patients over sixty has effectively run many tests, one per subgroup, and reported the lucky one. Unless the subgroup was specified in advance with a stated rationale, the finding is a hypothesis to test next, not a conclusion to act on now.

A permutation test makes few assumptions about the shape of the data. It does not need normality or equal variances, because the null distribution is built by reshuffling the actual observations rather than by invoking a theoretical curve. The price is computation, and the reward is a p-value that holds even when the textbook parametric assumptions plainly fail.

Splitting a continuous variable into groups at a cutoff chosen to maximize significance is a subtle dredge. The analyst tries the median split, then the tertile split, then a cutoff at a convenient round number, and presents whichever yielded the cleanest result. The cutoff was tuned to the data, and the p-value should be discounted accordingly.

A meta-analysis of published trials can overstate a drug's benefit because trials with null or negative results are less likely to reach print. The literature that the analyst can see is a survivorship-filtered slice of all trials run. Funnel plots and registries exist precisely to estimate the size of the missing, unflattering studies that never survived the editorial gate.

An insurance policy has negative expected value for the buyer; the premium exceeds the expected payout, since the insurer must profit. Buying it is still rational when the rare loss would be unbearable. The buyer trades a small certain cost for protection against a tail outcome, accepting a worse expectation in exchange for a tolerable worst case.

A graphical view makes the reversal vivid. Plot the outcome against the exposure for each subgroup and the within-group lines all slope upward. Connect the subgroup centroids and that line slopes downward, because the subgroups sit at staggered positions along both axes. The aggregate slope traces the arrangement of the clouds, while the within-group slopes describe the relationship inside them, and these need not agree.

The bootstrap shines for statistics with no clean theory, such as the median, a trimmed mean, or a ratio of two quantities. Where the central limit theorem offers no guidance, resampling builds the uncertainty estimate empirically. A confidence interval for the median, awkward to derive analytically, falls out of a few thousand bootstrap replications with little effort.

A sensitivity analysis for missing data deliberately varies the assumption about why values are absent and watches how the conclusion moves. If the result holds across a range of plausible missingness mechanisms, it is robust. If it depends delicately on assuming the gaps are benign, the honest report flags that dependence rather than hiding it behind a single imputation.

Roll one die and the outcomes are flat across one through six. Average ten dice and the distribution of that average already humps in the middle, with extremes rare. The central limit theorem promises this: sums and means of many independent contributions drift toward a bell shape regardless of the lumpy distribution each contribution was drawn from.

A quantile-quantile plot checks normality by plotting the data's quantiles against those of a normal distribution. If the points hug a straight line, normality is plausible. Systematic curvature at the ends reveals heavy or light tails, and an S-shape betrays skew. The plot diagnoses the specific way the data depart from the bell curve.

A doctor begins with a prior belief that a patient has a particular infection, perhaps a one-in-twenty chance given the symptoms. A test comes back positive. The posterior belief is the prior multiplied by how much more likely a positive result is under infection than under health, then renormalized. Belief moves in proportion to the strength of the evidence, anchored by where it started.

The breakdown point measures how much contamination a statistic can absorb before it becomes meaningless. The mean has a breakdown point of zero: a single bad value sent to infinity drags the mean with it. The median's breakdown point is one half; nearly half the data must be corrupted before it fails. Robust methods are chosen for high breakdown points.

A dashboard tracks fifty metrics and alerts whenever any crosses a control limit. Even in a perfectly stable system, watching fifty metrics means false alarms arrive routinely, because each metric has its own small chance of an excursion. Tuning the alert thresholds without accounting for how many things are being watched guarantees a steady drip of cries that mean nothing.

A run of bad luck in a casino, a string of plane incidents in one month, a cluster of system crashes, each invites a search for a cause. But if the events are genuinely rare and independent, their timing is irregular by nature, and bunching is expected somewhere in a long enough record. The statistical question is whether the bunching exceeds what randomness alone would deliver.

Partial autocorrelation isolates the direct link between an observation and one at a given lag, removing the influence of the intervening points. Where the ordinary autocorrelation at lag three may be inflated by the chain running through lags one and two, the partial version asks what lag three adds on its own, which is what model selection actually needs.

The atomistic fallacy is the mirror image: inferring a group-level relationship from individual data. Knowing how income relates to health within a city does not reveal how a city's average income relates to its average health, because contextual effects, the wealth of the surrounding community, operate at the group level and are invisible in the individual data.

When more than two raters score the same items, Fleiss's kappa generalizes the measure, summarizing how much a whole panel concurs beyond chance. A low value flags that the rating scheme itself is ambiguous, and the remedy is usually clearer guidelines or training rather than a search for the one rater out of step.

If a distribution has no finite mean, the law of large numbers in its standard form does not apply. Average draws from such a distribution and the running average wanders forever rather than settling. The law is a theorem with hypotheses, and a distribution wild enough to lack a mean can violate the very promise that the law is famous for.

The standard deviation returns the spread to the original units, where the variance, being a square, does not. A height dataset with a variance of nine square inches has a standard deviation of three inches, a figure one can picture against an actual person. The variance is mathematically convenient; the standard deviation is what communicates.

When a flight instructor praises a smooth landing and the next is worse, then scolds a rough landing and the next is better, the instructor concludes that criticism works and praise backfires. Both sequences are explained by ordinary regression toward each pilot's average. The intervention is applied precisely at the extremes, where the subsequent value almost always moves inward regardless of what the instructor said.

Analysis of variance earns its name by partitioning the total spread into a part explained by the groups and a part left within them. If the between-group variation dwarfs the within-group variation, the groups truly differ; if not, the apparent differences could be sampling noise. The whole inference is a comparison of two slices of variance.

A help line concludes its service is excellent because exit surveys are glowing. But callers who hung up in frustration, or who never got through, are absent from those surveys entirely. The instrument samples only the completed, patient interactions. Satisfaction measured this way is conditioned on having stayed long enough to be asked, which is exactly the population most likely to be content.

Expected value calculations are only as trustworthy as the probabilities fed into them. A business case projecting a handsome expected return collapses if the assumed success probability was optimistic guesswork. The arithmetic is exact; the inputs are estimates, and a confident expected value built on shaky probabilities offers false precision.

Data go missing in three broadly different ways, and the difference governs what an analyst can safely do. When missingness is unrelated to anything, a complete-case analysis is merely less efficient. When it depends on observed variables, it can be corrected by modeling. When it depends on the missing value itself, no method fully repairs the damage, and the analysis must lean on untestable assumptions.

Test-retest reliability asks whether the same subjects measured twice get consistent scores. A questionnaire that yields wildly different results from one week to the next, with nothing changed in between, is measuring noise. No matter how clever the analysis downstream, an unreliable instrument cannot support firm conclusions, because it does not reliably measure anything.

A lottery ticket costs two units and pays a million with probability one in five million. The expected payout is a fifth of a unit, so the expected value of the ticket is minus one point eight. Buy the ticket repeatedly and the law of large numbers turns that expectation into an almost certain steady loss, whatever a lucky night might suggest.

The p-value is a random variable. Run the identical experiment again, with a true effect present, and the value you get will scatter widely from run to run, even with reasonable power. A first study at 0.002 and a replication at 0.2 are not necessarily in conflict; that spread is exactly what sampling theory predicts. Treating any single p-value as a fixed property of the phenomenon misreads its nature.

Multilevel models address the problem by modeling both levels at once. Individuals are nested within groups, and the model estimates how outcomes depend on individual traits and on group context separately. This keeps the within-group relationship distinct from the between-group relationship, instead of collapsing them into one ambiguous correlation.

Poor interrater agreement contaminates everything downstream. If two coders label text data inconsistently, any analysis built on those labels inherits the noise, attenuating real relationships and inflating uncertainty. Reporting kappa before reporting results is a way of telling the reader how much trust the labels themselves can bear.

A kappa of one means perfect agreement, zero means agreement no better than chance, and a negative value means the raters disagree more than chance would predict. The intermediate range has no universal cutoff, though rough conventions call values above six-tenths substantial. Those labels are conventions, not facts, and the acceptable level depends on the stakes of the rating.

Two hospitals are compared on survival rates, and the one with the higher overall rate looks safer. But that hospital admits mostly routine cases, while the other is a referral center receiving the gravely ill. Within each severity tier the referral center may save more lives. The unadjusted comparison rewards the hospital that treats easier patients, a reversal that vanishes once case severity enters the calculation.

When a population has infinite variance, the classical central limit theorem simply does not apply. Averaging draws from such a distribution does not converge to a bell curve; the sample mean can remain as wild as a single observation. The theorem is powerful but conditional, and heavy-tailed phenomena like certain financial returns can violate its premises.

Replacing every gap with the column mean is tempting and almost always wrong. Mean imputation distorts the distribution, shrinking its variance and weakening every correlation with that variable. The dataset looks complete and tidy, but the analysis run on it carries a hidden bias toward zero relationships and overstated precision.

Acquiescence bias is the tendency to agree with whatever a question proposes. A questionnaire built entirely of statements phrased so that agreement means yes will collect inflated agreement. Balanced scales, mixing positively and negatively worded items, catch the respondents who are simply nodding along rather than reading.

A family has two children, and at least one is a girl. The probability that both are girls is one third, not one half, because the relevant sample space is the set of two-child families with at least one girl, of which only a third have two. The condition reshapes the space of possibilities, and counting within the reshaped space gives the surprising answer.

Two time series can correlate strongly simply because both trend upward over the years. Divorce rates and margarine consumption, or cheese eaten and deaths by bedsheet entanglement, have produced eerily tight curves. With enough candidate series, some pair will track another by accident. A correlation between trending variables carries almost no causal information until the trend is removed.

Apparent clusters of a rare disease in a small town often need no special cause. Scatter rare events at random across many towns and, by chance, some town will collect an unusual number. The cluster looks alarming until one remembers how many towns there were to throw the dice. Distinguishing a real hotspot from random clumping requires comparing against what pure chance would produce.

The log-rank test compares two survival curves by accumulating, at each event time, the gap between observed and expected events under the hypothesis of no difference. It weighs every point on the timeline, so two curves that cross can produce a non-significant result even though they differ sharply, because early and late differences partly cancel.

Clustered and repeated-measures designs change the power calculation. When observations within a cluster are correlated, the effective sample size is smaller than the head count suggests, and a naive power analysis assuming independence overstates the study's sensitivity. The design effect, driven by the intraclass correlation, must inflate the required sample accordingly.

The median survival time, the point where the Kaplan-Meier curve crosses one half, is often more meaningful than the mean. The mean survival can be undefined or unstable when many subjects are censored before the event, since the tail of the curve is never fully observed. The median needs only the curve to reach fifty percent, which it usually does.

A mixture distribution models a population built from distinct subgroups, each with its own distribution. Human heights are roughly a mixture of two near-normal components, one per sex. Fitting a single distribution to a mixture blurs the components into an awkward shape, while modeling the mixture explicitly recovers the structure and the proportion in each group.

Household income is the textbook right-skewed distribution. A long tail of high earners pulls the mean well above the median, so the average income exceeds what a typical household actually receives. Reporting the mean alone flatters the picture; the median, the income of the household in the middle, is the figure most people would recognize as typical.

Towns with more storks tend to have more births, a correlation once offered half-seriously as evidence for the legend. Larger towns simply have both more chimneys for storks and more residents to bear children. Population is the lurking variable, and the stork association evaporates once towns of comparable size are compared.

Independence is the fragile assumption behind many rare-event calculations. The chance of two unrelated failures is the product of their individual chances only if they truly are unrelated. Common causes, shared suppliers, or a single power outage can couple supposedly independent systems, and the joint failure probability can then dwarf the comfortable product the engineers computed.

Cramer's V rescales the chi-squared statistic into a measure of association strength bounded between zero and one. Because the raw chi-squared grows with sample size, a huge sample can make a trivial association significant; Cramer's V strips that out, reporting how tightly the categories are coupled independent of how many observations were counted.

Plotting residuals against a variable not in the model can reveal a missing predictor. If the residuals trend systematically with that left-out variable, the model has unexplained structure that the variable would capture. The residual plot becomes a diagnostic for what the model forgot, pointing toward the term that should have been included.

A profiling algorithm reports a ninety percent hit rate on a watch list, and officials call it accurate. But if the behavior it targets is extremely rare, the people correctly flagged are dwarfed by the innocents wrongly flagged. The headline accuracy describes performance on the rare positives; the experience of the population is governed by how often the common negatives are misclassified.

Customer data describe only the customers, not the people who looked and walked away. Analyzing why buyers chose a product cannot reveal why non-buyers did not, because non-buyers left no rows. Conclusions about appeal drawn purely from the purchaser dataset are conditioned on having purchased, and the most informative comparison group is absent by construction.

A study of half a million people finds that a dietary change lowers risk by an amount so small that p is below 0.0001. The significance is overwhelming and the effect is trivial. With a sample that large, almost any non-zero difference becomes statistically significant, so the relevant question shifts from whether there is an effect to whether the effect is big enough to act on.

Two events are independent when knowing one occurred tells you nothing about the chance of the other. The chance of both is then simply the product of their individual chances. This multiplication rule is the workhorse of probability, but it holds only under independence, and applying it to dependent events is one of the most common quantitative errors.

For dependent data the ordinary bootstrap breaks, because resampling individual points destroys the correlation structure. The block bootstrap repairs this by resampling contiguous chunks of the series, preserving the short-range dependence within each block. The block length is a tuning choice, long enough to capture the memory, short enough to leave many blocks to resample.

A boxplot shows the median, the quartiles, and the candidate outliers in a compact form, ideal for comparing many groups side by side. But it hides the shape within the box. A boxplot cannot distinguish a uniform spread from a sharply bimodal one, and where the within-group shape matters, a violin plot or a strip of raw points serves better.

Counting events that arrive rarely and independently over an interval, the number of customers in a minute, the typos on a page, calls for the Poisson distribution. Its single parameter is both its mean and its variance, a rigid constraint. When real count data show variance well above the mean, the Poisson is the wrong model and overdispersion must be accommodated.

A skewed distribution can hide a meaningful mixture. If a dataset of response times shows a bump of fast answers and a long tail of slow ones, the skew may reflect two underlying populations, those who knew the answer and those who guessed. The aggregate shape is then a clue, and modeling it as a mixture recovers structure that a single skewed curve would blur.

Ignoring a real interaction does not just lose detail; it can produce a model that fits no one. Averaging a positive effect in one group and a negative effect in another yields a near-zero coefficient that misrepresents both groups. A model with an interaction respects the heterogeneity; a model without it imposes a single effect that the data flatly contradict.

Goodness-of-fit testing checks whether a chosen distribution actually matches the data. A quantile plot, a chi-squared test on binned counts, or a Kolmogorov-Smirnov comparison can all expose a mismatch. A model resting on an unchecked distributional assumption may produce tidy output that quietly misrepresents the tails where decisions are most sensitive.

A skewed population leaves a fingerprint on the sample mean's distribution even after the bell shape emerges: convergence proceeds faster in the center than in the tails. So a confidence interval built on the normal approximation may have decent coverage near the middle while being noticeably off for extreme quantiles, which matters when the question concerns rare outcomes.

Reacting to every wiggle in a noisy series is a recognized failure mode, sometimes illustrated by adjusting a process in response to random fluctuation, which only adds variance. The discipline is to change the process in response to a confirmed signal and to leave it alone when the movement is within the band of ordinary noise.

When strata are sampled at different rates, the analysis must reweight. A rare subgroup oversampled to ensure enough respondents would, if simply averaged in, dominate the estimate out of proportion to its true share. Survey weights inversely proportional to the selection probability restore each stratum to its rightful population fraction.

Conditioning on a collider can manufacture a dependence between truly independent causes. If a celebrity is famous either for talent or for beauty, then among celebrities the two traits appear negatively correlated, even if they are unrelated in the general population. Restricting attention to those who made it conditions on the common effect and bends the joint distribution.

The interquartile range, the width of the middle half of the data, ignores the extremes and so resists outliers. It pairs naturally with the median, and together they describe a skewed or contaminated distribution far more honestly than a mean and standard deviation, which an extreme tail can both inflate and distort.

The human mind handles rare-event probabilities poorly, treating one-in-a-thousand and one-in-a-million as both simply unlikely. Yet they differ by a factor of a thousand, and a decision that hinges on the difference, an insurance premium, a safety margin, a screening policy, cannot afford the blur. Calibration against frequencies, not adjectives, is the corrective.

Stratified sampling can also serve fairness rather than mere precision. A national survey may deliberately oversample a small minority so that subgroup-level estimates are reliable, accepting some loss of efficiency for the overall figure. The design encodes a choice about which questions the survey is meant to answer well.

Proportional allocation gives each stratum a sample share equal to its population share. Optimal allocation does better, sending more of the sample to strata that are both large and internally variable, and fewer to strata that are small or uniform. The optimal scheme minimizes the overall variance for a fixed total sample by spending observations where they buy the most precision.

A truncated vertical axis exaggerates differences. A bar chart starting at ninety rather than zero can make a two-percent gap look like a chasm. The visualization is technically accurate yet rhetorically dishonest, and a careful viewer always checks where the axis begins before trusting the magnitude a chart appears to show.

With only six observations, the sample standard deviation is a shaky estimate, and treating the sample mean as if it followed a normal curve understates the uncertainty. The t-distribution, with its heavier tails, was devised for exactly this situation, widening the confidence interval to account for the extra noise in estimating the spread from so few points.

subtopic: Type I and Type II errors
sentence: Increasing the sample size is the one move that lowers both error rates together. With more data the sampling distributions of the test statistic under the null and the alternative pull apart, so the same threshold catches more true effects while flagging no more true nulls. Every other adjustment merely trades one error for the other; only information buys down both.

P-hacking is rarely fraud; it is usually a sincere analyst who believes an effect is there and keeps adjusting until the data agree. That sincerity is what makes it insidious. The corrective is structural, not moral: procedures that constrain analytic freedom, so that the result does not depend on a researcher's hopeful nudging of the knobs.

Assuming independence where it does not hold makes uncertainty look smaller than it is. If two risks share a hidden common cause, their joint failure probability far exceeds the product the independence assumption predicts. Many engineering and financial disasters trace back to a multiplication of supposedly independent small probabilities that were, in truth, coupled.

Guarding against the fallacy means always asking what population the probability lives in and which direction the conditional runs. The probability of the evidence given a hypothesis is the building block; the probability of the hypothesis given the evidence is the goal. Reaching the goal requires a prior and an explicit comparison, and any argument that skips them is incomplete however small its quoted number.

There are several ways to turn bootstrap replications into a confidence interval. The simplest reads off the percentiles of the resampled statistics. More refined approaches correct for bias and skewness in the bootstrap distribution. The choice matters most when the statistic's distribution is far from symmetric, where the naive percentile interval can be noticeably off.

Cats falling from greater heights were reported to suffer fewer injuries, prompting talk of a relaxing reflex. A simpler reading is that cats killed by long falls are less likely to be carried to a veterinary clinic and recorded. The dataset is conditioned on the cat arriving alive, so the most catastrophic outcomes are missing from the high-fall rows.

A residual that is far larger than the rest flags an observation the model fits badly. It may be a data error, or a genuine case the model's structure cannot accommodate. Either way it deserves inspection, because a single large residual can also be exerting outsized leverage, quietly bending the fitted line toward itself.

To test whether a treatment shifts an outcome, shuffle the treatment labels across subjects thousands of times and recompute the difference in means under each shuffle. If the genuine, unshuffled difference sits far out in the tail of those shuffled differences, the labels carry real signal. The test asks how surprising the observed gap is against a world where the labels meant nothing.

A study finds that districts with higher average screen time have lower average test scores and warns parents about screens harming children. The data are aggregated by district, so they cannot identify which children used screens or which scored poorly. The pattern is consistent with screens being harmless and concentrated in districts that score low for unrelated reasons.

A permutation test for a correlation pairs each x with a randomly reassigned y, breaking any genuine link while preserving each variable's marginal distribution. Repeating this many times yields the spread of correlations expected under no association. The observed correlation is then judged against that spread, and its rank gives the p-value directly.

Power rises with the sample size, with the true effect size, and with lower variability, and falls as the significance threshold is tightened. Detecting a subtle effect against noisy measurements demands a large sample; the same effect measured cleanly needs fewer subjects. Power analysis makes these trades explicit so the design is neither wastefully large nor hopelessly small.

The bootstrap can estimate bias as well as variance. If the average of the bootstrap replications drifts away from the statistic computed on the full sample, that drift estimates the bias of the statistic itself. Subtracting it yields a bias-corrected estimate, a correction obtained by computation where an analytic derivation would be forbidding.

When a composite score is built from many items, internal consistency, often summarized by Cronbach's alpha, gauges whether the items hang together as measures of one underlying trait. A low alpha warns that the items may be tapping different things, so summing them produces a number whose meaning is muddled and whose reliability is poor.

Cluster sampling trades precision for cost. Rather than scattering interviewers across a whole city, the surveyor randomly selects a few neighborhoods and canvasses each thoroughly. Travel is cheap, but people within a neighborhood resemble one another, so each respondent adds less fresh information, and the effective sample size falls below the head count.

Reporting only that a difference was significant withholds the most useful information. Significant tells the reader the data are inconsistent with exactly zero effect. It does not say whether the effect is a faint nudge or a dramatic shift. The effect size answers that, and an analysis that omits it leaves the audience unable to judge importance.

If subjects can sense their assignment, randomization alone is not enough. A patient who knows they received the active drug may report symptoms differently, reintroducing bias through expectation. Blinding the subjects, and ideally the assessors, keeps the assignment hidden so that the only systematic difference between arms remains the treatment under test.

Traffic authorities install cameras at intersections that recorded the most accidents last year, then point to the drop the next year as proof the cameras work. Accident counts at any site swing widely, and a site is chosen precisely because it had an unlucky year. Some decline was coming anyway. A credible evaluation must compare against intersections with similarly bad histories that received no camera.

Skewness has a sign. Income is right-skewed, with the tail toward high values. Age at death in a developed country is left-skewed, with most people dying old and a tail reaching back toward early deaths. The direction of the tail matters for which summary overstates the typical case and for which extreme events the model must be prepared to expect.

A rookie athlete who posts a spectacular debut season tends to disappoint the next year, and commentators reach for sophomore slump as an explanation. The simpler account is that the debut was an upward fluctuation around the player's true ability, and fluctuations of that size do not recur on schedule. The decline is the expected return toward the long-run mean, not a psychological collapse demanding narrative.

The intuitive reading most people give a confidence interval, that the parameter is probably inside it, is actually the definition of a credible interval. The frequentist machinery does not license that reading, which is why the credible interval feels more natural. The price of that naturalness is the need to specify a prior.

Averaging repeated measurements reduces random error, because the noise partly cancels while the signal accumulates. Three readings of a blood pressure, averaged, are more reliable than one. The improvement follows the square-root law, so the gains diminish, but for a noisy instrument a few repeats can lift reliability from inadequate to usable.

Multistage sampling layers the two ideas. First sample provinces, within chosen provinces sample districts, within chosen districts sample households, within chosen households sample one person. Each stage is a cluster step, and the cumulative design effect can be substantial. The variance estimate must walk back up the same hierarchy that the sampling walked down.

Independence is the assumption that the central limit theorem and most standard error formulas quietly rely on. Observations drawn in correlated clusters, or measured repeatedly on the same subject, are not independent, and the effective sample size is smaller than the count. Treating such data as independent yields confidence intervals narrower than the data can honestly support.

Estimating wildlife abundance by counting animals seen along roads undercounts species that avoid roads and overcounts those drawn to them. The roadside is a biased window onto the habitat. A defensible estimate requires either a sampling design that covers the landscape evenly or an explicit model of how detectability varies with distance from the road.

A frequent slip is to read the p-value as the probability that the observed result occurred by chance. Under the null hypothesis the result occurred by chance with probability one, since the null says chance is all there is. The p-value instead reports how far into the tail the data fell on that assumption. The chance explanation is the premise of the calculation, not its conclusion.

How a question is worded shapes the answer it collects. Asking whether the government should forbid speeches against democracy draws more permissive responses than asking whether it should allow them, though the two are logically equivalent. The framing nudges the respondent, and a survey that uses only one framing measures the wording as much as the opinion.

A magazine polls its readers about a policy and reports overwhelming support. The result describes the magazine's readership, not the public. People who subscribe, who notice the survey, and who bother to mail it back differ systematically from everyone who did not. The sampling frame and the response process together select a slice of opinion that no honest headline can call representative of the nation.

A credible interval depends on the prior, and that dependence is a feature, not a flaw, provided the prior is honest. Two analysts with different priors will report different credible intervals from the same data, and each is correct relative to its prior. The confidence interval avoids this by refusing to put a probability on the parameter at all.

Neither interval is universally superior; they answer different questions and rest on different philosophies. The confidence interval offers a guarantee that holds without a prior, attractive when no prior is defensible. The credible interval offers a direct probability statement, attractive when a decision must be made. Knowing which question is being asked decides which interval to report.

Stacking two studies, one with p equal to 0.04 and one with p equal to 0.06, people conclude the first replicated and the second did not. But two estimates can have nearly identical effect sizes and overlapping intervals while straddling the threshold purely through sampling noise. The comparison that matters is between the effect estimates and their uncertainty, not between the labels significant and non-significant pinned to each.

Independence is a load-bearing assumption. If observations are correlated, as in a time series or a clustered sample, the effective number of independent pieces of information is smaller than the raw count, and the sample mean converges more slowly than the theorem's standard form suggests. Treating correlated data as independent makes confidence intervals too narrow.

Selecting which interval to report after seeing several can break the coverage guarantee. If an analyst computes intervals for ten outcomes and presents the one that excludes zero, that interval no longer has ninety-five percent coverage in any meaningful sense. The guarantee holds for the procedure as a whole, including the rule for choosing what to report, not for a cherry-picked survivor.

A Monte Carlo simulation is only as good as its random number generator and its model. A flawed generator with hidden periodicity can correlate runs that should be independent, and a model that omits a real-world feature will simulate a world that does not exist. Validating both is essential before trusting the count of wins.

The theorem is why the standard error of the mean shrinks with the square root of the sample size and why so many test statistics are referred to a normal table. It quietly underwrites the z-test, much of the t-test, and the normal approximation to the binomial. A great deal of routine inference rests on this single limiting result holding well enough at the sample sizes in hand.

Markov chain Monte Carlo extends the idea to sampling from distributions too complex to draw from directly. Rather than independent draws, it builds a chain of dependent samples that, after a settling-in period, wander through the distribution in the right proportions. It is the workhorse that made Bayesian computation practical for models of real complexity.

An event with a one-in-a-million chance per attempt is nearly certain to occur somewhere if there are a hundred million attempts. Rare per trial does not mean rare overall. Lottery jackpots are won regularly precisely because so many tickets are sold, and the same arithmetic explains why freak coincidences happen to someone every day.

A z-score restates a raw value as the number of standard deviations it lies from the mean. A test result two standard deviations above average becomes a z-score of two regardless of the original units. This common scale lets a height, a temperature, and an exam mark be compared on equal footing, each translated into its position within its own distribution.

Mutual fund performance tables flatter the industry because closed and merged funds drop out of the database. The poor performers vanish, and the average return of the survivors overstates what an investor could have expected at the outset. A fair estimate must include the funds that died, since at decision time the investor could not know which ones would.

Average wait times can mislead when the distribution is skewed. A call center reporting a mean wait of four minutes may have most callers answered in under a minute and a few stuck for half an hour. The mean is pulled by the unlucky tail. A service-level statistic, the fraction of callers answered within a target, captures the experience the mean obscures.

Flip a fair coin ten times and a run of eight heads would not astonish anyone. Flip it ten thousand times and the proportion of heads will sit close to one half, with deviations of that size now vanishingly rare. The law of large numbers promises that the sample proportion converges to the true probability as the trials accumulate.

A trimmed mean discards a fixed fraction of the smallest and largest values before averaging the rest. It keeps much of the efficiency of the ordinary mean when the data are well behaved, yet resists a handful of wild points. The trimming fraction is a dial between sensitivity to all the data and protection against its extremes.

Confounding can flip a result's sign, not merely shrink it. An observational study can show a treatment associated with worse outcomes when in truth it helps, simply because the sicker patients were the ones who received it. This confounding by indication is endemic in medical data, and it is why a positive observational signal so often fails to survive a randomized trial.

The gambler who expects a red after a long run of black has confused the law of large numbers with a memory the wheel does not have. Each spin is independent; past outcomes do not tilt the next. Convergence of the long-run frequency happens because future trials dwarf the early imbalance, not because the wheel owes the gambler anything.

subtopic: Type I and Type II errors
sentence: Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null, one minus the Type II error rate. A study with thirty percent power will miss a real effect seven times in ten. Running such a study and reporting a non-significant result as evidence of no effect mistakes a near-blindfolded test for a clear-eyed one.

Paired categorical data, such as a diagnosis before and after a change, call for McNemar's test rather than the ordinary chi-squared. The interest lies only in the discordant pairs, the subjects who changed category. The concordant pairs carry no information about a shift, so the test focuses on the off-diagonal counts where the change actually shows.

A study of eight patients that reports a confidence interval running from a small harm to a large benefit has not failed; it has honestly shown that eight patients cannot resolve the question. Small samples produce wide intervals, and a wide interval is the correct expression of how little the data constrain the answer.

A witness who correctly identifies cab colors eighty percent of the time reports a blue cab in a city where only fifteen percent of cabs are blue. Folding in the base rate, the probability the cab was actually blue is closer to forty percent than to eighty. The witness's reliability is real, but it operates against a backdrop where blue cabs are uncommon, and that backdrop cannot be set aside.

Decision trees compute expected value by folding back from the outcomes. Each chance node is replaced by the probability-weighted average of its branches, each decision node by the best branch, and the calculation rolls back to the root. The result is the expected value of the optimal strategy, a single number summarizing a tangle of contingent choices.

An odds ratio is not a risk ratio, though headlines routinely treat them as one. When the outcome is rare the two nearly coincide, but when the outcome is common the odds ratio exaggerates. A study reporting an odds ratio of three for a frequent outcome may correspond to a risk ratio closer to one and a half, and the difference matters for the reader.

Smokers in a long-running survey appeared to have better twenty-year survival than non-smokers, an absurd headline until age was introduced. The non-smokers skewed much older, since many lifelong non-smokers were already elderly at enrollment. Within each age band smokers fared worse, as expected. The naive comparison let age masquerade as a smoking effect, and stratifying restored the sensible direction.

A histogram's story depends on its bin width. Too few bins smooth real structure into a single bland mound; too many shatter it into spiky noise. The honest practice is to view the data at several bin widths, because no single choice is neutral, and a bimodal distribution can hide entirely behind a poorly chosen bin size.

When the sampling distribution of a statistic resists a formula, the bootstrap simulates it. Treat the observed sample as a stand-in for the population, draw new samples from it with replacement, recompute the statistic on each, and the spread of those recomputed values approximates how the statistic would vary across real samples. The data become their own model of the population.

The likelihood ratio is the engine of the update: how much more probable the observed evidence is under one hypothesis than under its rival. A ratio of one leaves belief untouched; a ratio of ten multiplies the prior odds tenfold. Reading evidence this way separates the strength of a finding from whatever prior the analyst happened to bring.

When data are scarce, the prior dominates the credible interval, and that can be a strength or a danger. A well-justified prior stabilizes an estimate the data alone cannot pin down. A poorly justified prior smuggles in a conclusion. The honest practice is to report how much the interval would move under alternative reasonable priors.

An interaction is symmetric. Saying the effect of fertilizer depends on rainfall is the same statement as saying the effect of rainfall depends on fertilizer. The single interaction term captures both readings at once, and which framing to emphasize is a choice of exposition, not of statistics.

Treatment A outperforms treatment B for patients with small kidney stones and again for patients with large stones, yet B appears better when the two groups are pooled. Doctors steered the harder cases toward A, so A's overall numbers carry a heavier burden of severe patients. The pooled comparison confounds the treatment with the case mix, and only the stratified figures answer the clinical question.

The bootstrap embodies a shift in spirit: replace a hard probability calculation with brute-force simulation. Before fast computers, an analyst needed a closed-form sampling distribution to make progress. The bootstrap trades that mathematical demand for computational labor, and for a wide class of problems the trade is overwhelmingly favorable.

Anthropic selection effects shape what we can observe about the universe and ourselves. Any cosmos we find ourselves measuring must be one capable of producing observers, which biases the sample of universes to one. On a smaller scale, the same logic warns that any dataset we examine was, in some sense, available to be examined, and that availability is itself a filter.

When independent quantities are added, their variances add, not their standard deviations. Combine two processes each with a standard deviation of three and the sum has variance eighteen, hence a standard deviation near four point two, not six. This is why diversification reduces relative risk and why error propagation works through squared terms.

A hazard ratio, common in survival analysis, compares the instantaneous rate of an event between two groups, not the eventual cumulative risk. A hazard ratio of one half does not mean half as many people will eventually suffer the event; it means the event arrives at half the rate at any given moment, which translates into cumulative risk only through the whole survival curve.

A monthly sales figure that ticks up is not yet a trend. In any series with random fluctuation, consecutive values rise and fall by chance, and a single increase is as likely to reverse as to continue. Distinguishing a genuine trend from noise requires enough observations to see the signal emerge from the scatter, not a glance at the last two points.

Standardizing to z-scores does not change the shape of a distribution; it only shifts and rescales it. A skewed distribution converted to z-scores remains exactly as skewed. The transformation centers the data at zero with unit spread, which is convenient, but it cannot manufacture normality out of data that were never bell-shaped.

A ninety-five percent confidence interval does not mean there is a ninety-five percent probability the true parameter lies inside this particular interval. Once computed, the interval either contains the parameter or it does not; the probability is zero or one. The ninety-five percent describes the procedure: across many datasets, intervals built this way capture the parameter about ninety-five times in a hundred.

Voting studies are a classic trap. Counties with larger shares of a demographic group may lean toward a candidate, yet members of that group may vote the other way, with the county tilted by everyone else. The aggregate cannot reveal how the group itself voted; only a survey of individuals can, and treating the county pattern as the group's preference is the fallacy.

Sequential conditioning is the chain rule of probability. The chance of three events all occurring is the chance of the first, times the chance of the second given the first, times the chance of the third given both. Each factor narrows the world the next factor lives in, and the product walks through a sequence of progressively conditioned spaces.

Schools placed on a watch list for the worst test scores in one year frequently improve the following year, and the remediation program takes the credit. But selection on an extreme value guarantees some rebound by chance alone. Without a comparison group of similarly low-scoring schools left untreated, the design cannot separate the program's effect from the statistical pull back toward the district average.

Daily temperatures are not independent draws; a warm day is followed more often by a warm day than a cold one. This autocorrelation means a time series carries less information than its length suggests. Treating each day as an independent observation produces standard errors that are far too small and confidence in trends that the data do not support.

Regions with more immigrants show higher literacy rates, and one might conclude that immigrants are more literate.
